Yes, the story has an appropriate balance between scene and summary/exposition. 

The narrative primarily unfolds as a real-time scene on the ferry dock, using vivid sensory details (the coughing engine, the dripping steel cable, the suitcase wheel catching in the wooden planks), physical actions, and natural dialogue between Ilse and her son, Jonas. Woven seamlessly into this scene are brief, well-placed moments of exposition and summary. Instead of halting the story with long backstory dumps, the writer uses details in the immediate environment—like Jonas's city clothes, the familiar sounds of the ferry, and Henning's blue mug on the windowsill—to naturally deliver character history and imply the recent loss of Henning. This balance keeps the pacing engaging while giving the reader all the emotional context needed to understand the weight of the moment.
